conventions.convention: Divergence is defined on C¹ fields U→Rⁿ for n≥1, while curl is defined only in R³ with x,y,z denoting indices 0,1,2 and curl F=(∂yFz−∂zFy, ∂zFx−∂xFz, ∂xFy−∂yFx).

The cyclic projections are πx(p)=(py,pz), πy(p)=(pz,px), and πz(p)=(px,py). A simple solid has a compact Jordan base with nonempty interior and continuous graph functions satisfying γ1≤γ2 on the base and γ1<γ2 on its interior.

A unit vector ν is outward at p when, for all sufficiently small t>0, p+tν lies outside the compact solid and p−tν lies inside it. Uniqueness is asserted only relative to a supplied two-dimensional tangent plane.

An adapted presentation partitions one fixed patch list into upper, lower, and lateral sublists: the kth oriented-area coordinate is respectively positive, negative, or zero on parameter interiors; the projected interiors of each graph sublist are pairwise disjoint and fill the base up to content zero; both graph sublists are nonempty.
An elementary solid carries three supplied simple descriptions but one common compatible boundary-patch presentation; only the upper/lower/lateral partition changes with coordinate direction.

For classical Stokes, the parameter region is a supplied finite elementary Green region, its positive boundary chain is transported through the C² parametrization, and the surface orientation is induced by φu×φv. The pointwise integrand identity itself does not require patch regularity.

Half-open boxes use (ai,bi], not [ai,bi), with extended-real parameters. An empty box has volume 0; a nonempty box with an infinite endpoint has volume +∞; otherwise its volume is the product of its positive side lengths.
Dyadic generations are natural numbers beginning at k=0; Qk,m=∏i(mi2^−k,(mi+1)2^−k], so generation 0 consists of integer translates of (0,1]ⁿ and there are no coarser negative generations.

The construction assumes the Axiom of Countable Choice from the assertion that the induced set function is an outer measure onward. Under that assumption λn is complete, contains every elementary set, and extends elementary volume.
For a singular linear map, the change-of-variables conclusion is stated as λn(T[E])=0 for every E, not as |det T|λn(E), because 0·(+∞) is undefined in the library's extended-real arithmetic.
The winding number is n(γ,p)=(2πi)⁻¹∫γ dz/(z−p) for a parametrized closed rectifiable contour and a point off its trace. It depends on traversal multiplicity and direction, not merely on the trace.

A complex chain is a finite list of integer-weighted contours, not an element of a free abelian group. Zero-coefficient terms are excluded from its trace, and it is a cycle exactly when its endpoint boundary function vanishes identically.
A cycle Γ in an open Ω is null-homologous in Ω exactly when n(Γ,p)=0 for every p outside Ω; homology means equality of those indices outside Ω, not equality of chain lists.
Cᵐ is identified with R²ᵐ in the interleaved order (x0,y0,x1,y1,…), and every coordinate and multi-index starts at 0.

Several-variable holomorphy means complex Fréchet differentiability with a C-linear differential. Continuity and local boundedness are consequences or extra hypotheses, not part of the definition; separate holomorphy likewise includes no joint continuity.

The distinguished boundary of a polydisc requires every coordinate to lie on its circle; for m≥2 it is strictly smaller than the topological boundary. The polydisc Cauchy formula is an iterated contour integral in the displayed order, not an integral over a product boundary.
The several-variable identity theorem assumes vanishing on a nonempty open subset of a connected open domain; a zero set with merely an accumulation point is insufficient.

load_bearing.statement: For n≥1 and a C¹ field F:U→Rⁿ, div F=∑i<n ∂iFi. For n=3, curl F=(∂yFz−∂zFy, ∂zFx−∂xFz, ∂xFy−∂yFx), with x,y,z denoting coordinates 0,1,2.

Assuming the Axiom of Countable Choice, L(Rⁿ) is a sigma-algebra, λn is a complete measure on it, every outer-null subset is measurable and null, and every elementary set is measurable with λn(A)=μ0(A).

For m≥1, Cᵐ is identified with R²ᵐ by z↦(x0,y0,…,x(m−1),y(m−1)); the Euclidean norms agree, so metric, convergence, continuity, completeness, compactness, openness, and connectedness are read through this interleaved identification.
For n≥1 and extended-real parameters a,b, B(a,b)={x∈Rⁿ: ai<xi≤bi for all i<n}. Its volume is 0 when empty, +∞ when nonempty with an infinite endpoint, and ∏i<n(bi−ai) when all endpoints are real.

A complex chain in an open Ω is a finite list ((m0,γ0),…,(m(r−1),γ(r−1))) of integer-weighted contours with trace in Ω. Its trace excludes zero-coefficient terms; its boundary at q is the weighted sum of endpoints at q minus starting points at q; it is a cycle iff that boundary is zero for every q.
For a chain Γ=∑k<r mkγk and f continuous on Γ*, ∫Γ f dz=∑mk≠0 mk∫γk f dz. For p∉Γ*, n(Γ,p)=(2πi)⁻¹∫Γ dz/(z−p).
For a∈Cᵐ and positive polyradius r, Δr(a) requires |zk−ak|<rk in every coordinate, its closure uses ≤, and its distinguished boundary Γr(a) requires equality in every coordinate.
Assuming countable choice, for real ai≤bi every set R satisfying R°⊆R⊆[a,b] is Lebesgue measurable and λn(R)=∏i<n(bi−ai), independently of which faces are included.
For m≥1, f:U→C is complex differentiable at a when f(a+h)=f(a)+L(h)+r(h) for a C-linear L:Cᵐ→C and |r(h)|/‖h‖→0; it is holomorphic when this holds at every point.
A cycle Γ with trace in open Ω is null-homologous in Ω iff n(Γ,p)=0 for every p∈C∖Ω. Two cycles are homologous in Ω iff their indices agree at every point outside Ω.
A simple description (k,D,γ1,γ2) has D compact Jordan with nonempty interior, γ1,γ2 continuous, γ1≤γ2 on D and γ1<γ2 on D°, and describes E={p:πk(p)∈D, γ1(πk(p))≤pk≤γ2(πk(p))}.
For a closed rectifiable contour γ and p off its trace, n(γ,p)=(2πi)⁻¹∫γ dz/(z−p); the index is attached to the parametrized contour, not merely its trace.

An adapted compatible presentation is supplied with upper, lower, and lateral sublists whose kth oriented-area coordinates are positive, negative, and zero on parameter interiors; each graph sublist's projected interiors are pairwise disjoint and fill the base up to content zero; both graph sublists are nonempty.

For a supplied finite gluing of elementary solid regions with union E and outer boundary presentation, and a C¹ vector field on an open set containing E, ∭E div F=∬∂E⟨F,n⟩. The piece decomposition, patch designations, and internal pairings are hypotheses.

A C² patch over a finite elementary Green region is a regular patch whose compact parameter region carries a supplied finite elementary Green decomposition and whose parametrization is C² near that region. Its induced boundary chain is the image under φ of the positive parameter-boundary chain; circulation is the finite sum of vector line integrals along those image arcs.

If m≥1, U⊆Cᵐ is open, and f:U→C is continuous and separately holomorphic, then f is holomorphic. For continuous f, holomorphy, separate holomorphy, and local representation by absolutely convergent multi-indexed power series are equivalent.
If Ω⊆C is open, f is holomorphic on Ω, and Γ is a null-homologous cycle with trace in Ω, then for every z∈Ω∖Γ*, n(Γ,z)f(z)=(2πi)⁻¹∫Γ f(ζ)/(ζ−z)dζ; Ω need not be connected.

published_dependencies.used_for: Coordinate indexing, Euclidean norms, inner products, gradients, flux pairings, and the Cᵐ/R²ᵐ dictionary.
Fixes cross-product signs used by curl, oriented area vectors, Stokes, and vector identities.
Supplies the componentwise Cᵏ regularity convention for vector fields and parametrizations.
Supplies Jacobian matrices and gradients used throughout the divergence/curl and SCV developments.
Licenses mixed-partial exchanges in curl-gradient, divergence-curl, curl-curl, and the Stokes integrand identity.
Controls negligible parameter boundaries, projected residues, Jordan-piece overlaps, and comparison with Lebesgue nullity.
Base change-of-variables theorem used by coordinate permutations and extended locally to boundary-degenerate parametrizations.
Establishes the open image in the boundary-degenerate change-of-variables lemma and local graph coordinates for outward normals.
Fixes patch regularity, parameter-region conditions, and permitted boundary degeneracy.
Fixes the φu×φv orientation and the flux integrand.
Defines compatible finite presentations and the sums giving area, scalar integrals, and flux.
Makes paired internal faces cancel under orientation-reversing reparametrization.
The planar integral theorem from which the classical Stokes theorem is derived.
Fixes the sign and traversal order of parameter-boundary chains in Green and Stokes.
Computes volume and surface examples and the shrinking-disc area integrals.
Evaluates the one-dimensional inner integrals in flux, Green, and worked examples.
Names the precise choice assumption used from the Lebesgue outer-measure construction onward.
Fixes +∞ arithmetic and the undefined 0·(+∞) case that shapes the box and singular-map statements.
Supplies the countable-additivity and sigma-finiteness target for elementary volume.
Defines Lebesgue outer measure from elementary-cover costs.
Provides the countable-choice-dependent outer-measure axioms for λn*.
Produces the measurable sigma-algebra and complete measure from λn*.
Shows elementary sets are measurable and λn extends elementary volume.
Identifies the Lebesgue sigma-algebra as the completion of Borel Lebesgue measure.
Confirms the (a,b] half-open convention and identifies the Borel generators.
Fixes the Borel sigma-algebra used in measurability, uniqueness, and completion results.
Proves uniqueness of normalized translation-invariant Borel measure from dyadic/open-set values.
Reduces the determinant scaling constant to coordinate scalings, permutations, and shears.
Identifies the multiplicative Lebesgue scaling constant with |det T|.
Transfers elementary nullity through Lipschitz maps and supports affine-subspace and linear-image results.
Fixes rectifiable contours, traces, reversal, concatenation, and closedness for winding numbers and chains.
Defines the line integrals underlying winding numbers, chain integration, and Cauchy formulas.
Ensures continuous kernels and integrands are integrable along the page's rectifiable contours.
Controls tagged-sum errors, continuity of the index, decay of Cauchy transforms, and several estimates.
Evaluates logarithmic-derivative and primitive integrals along contours and cycles.
Provides ker(exp)=2πiZ for logarithm uniqueness and integrality of winding numbers.
Supplies initial logarithm values and normalization of global holomorphic logarithms.
The one-variable slice formula iterated over polydiscs.
Shows parameter-integral limits and slice limits remain holomorphic.
Forces Dixon's glued entire function to vanish and proves the global Cauchy formula.
Converts vanishing integrals over closed contours into existence of a primitive.
Transfers topology and real Euclidean notions between C and R² and anchors the Cᵐ dictionary.
Provides the real Fréchet derivative compared with the complex-linear differential in several variables.
Ensures the real and complex readings of the differential agree when both apply.
Controls power-series coefficients and supplies the uniform slice-derivative bound behind locally bounded separate holomorphy.
Provides the one-variable identity theorem contrasted with the weaker several-variable form.
Applied to complex-line slices to prove the several-variable scalar maximum-modulus principle.
Applied to a nonconstant complex-line slice to prove the scalar several-variable open-mapping theorem.

concerns.concern: The Remark claiming that a cube corner admits no outward vector is false. At p=(1,1,1) on the cube [−1,1]³, ν=(1,1,1)/√3 satisfies p+tν∉E and p−tν∈E for every sufficiently small t>0.

The title calls the construction a figure-eight, but the Example explicitly uses two circles of radius 1/2 centred at −1 and 1 and proves their traces are disjoint. The index computation is correct for a disjoint two-circle chain, not for the figure-eight named by the title.

The unconditional Remark “A vector potential is never unique” overlooks the allowed empty open set U. On U=∅ there is only one map U→R³, hence only one vector potential. The argument gives nonuniqueness once U is nonempty.

The Statement begins with m,n≥1 and then appends a clause for n=0; the defining item likewise fixes n≥1 before discussing n=0 only in a Remark. The zero-target convention is therefore outside the quantified theorem rather than an actual case of it.
